title: Coping with Divots Drill
description: Setup: On the range, find a spot with decent turf. Use a 7-iron. Draw a line in the grass (or use spray paint/chalk) where the ball would be. Execution: Make swings focusing on taking SHALLOW divots that start AT or AFTER the line (ball position), not before it. The divot should be: (1) About the size of a dollar bill (not a crater), (2) Starting at ball position or slightly ahead, (3) Pointing at your target. Key technique: Maintain your spine angle through impact, keep weight shifting forward, and feel like you're 'brushing' the grass rather than chopping down. If your divots are deep or behind the line, you're likely hanging back or casting. Hit 20 balls, checking each divot location. Goal: 15+ divots starting at or after the ball line.

title: Tempo Feel — Ernie Els Rhythm
description: Say “Er‑nie Els” back and through to groove a smooth, unhurried cadence. Let the club swing you.

title: Carpet Putting Track Drill
description: Place two alignment sticks or clubs parallel on a carpet about a ball-width apart and roll putts between them; develops a square face and straight path at home.

title: Monitor the Strike Spray
description: Use foot spray on the driver face to see strike location; adjust your setup until strikes are centered to maximize distance and consistency.

title: Grip Pressure Check Drill
description: Hold the club as lightly as possible while still maintaining control; light grip pressure promotes clubhead speed and reduces tension.

title: Chopsticks Alignment Drill
description: Setup: Take two alignment sticks (or long dowels) and place them under your armpits, one on each side. Bind the front ends together with a rubber band so they form a 'V' shape pointing away from your chest. The sticks should rest against your upper arms/chest. Execution: Make putting strokes while keeping the sticks parallel to the ground and moving together. If one stick tilts up or down, your shoulders are tilting rather than rocking level. The sticks should move as a unit—both rotating together around your spine. Key insight: A proper putting stroke is driven by shoulder rotation, not hands/wrists. The chopsticks exaggerate any independent hand action or shoulder tilt. Practice 20-30 strokes without a ball first, then hit putts while maintaining the parallel stick position. Goal: Make 10 putts in a row with the sticks staying perfectly parallel throughout the stroke.

title: Control the Low Point Drill
description: Place a tee or coin just ahead of the ball and practise hitting the ground after the ball to control the low point of your swing for crisp iron shots.

title: Putting Drill — Gate and Start Line
description: Create a gate with two tees just wider than the putter face 6 inches in front of the ball. Roll 25 putts through the gate on your start line.

title: Throw the Basketball Down Feel
description: Imagine tossing a basketball down the target line during your downswing. Good drivers throw it down the line rather than into the ground, which helps shallow the club and prevent coming over the top.

title: Tempo Ladder Game
description:
Pick any club. Hit three balls at each “rung” of the ladder:
Rung 1: 30% effort — smooth and slow, just brush the grass.
Rung 2: 50% effort — same rhythm, a little more speed.
Rung 3: 70% effort — tempo still feels identical, just more flow.
Rung 4: 90% effort — powerful but controlled.
Rung 5: 100% — full swing, same rhythm you started with.

If a shot feels rushed or off-balance, drop back down one rung and rebuild.

Scoring / Challenge:
Make solid contact at every rung in a row — that’s a clean climb. BONUS: if you can climb and descend (100 → 30%) without losing tempo, you’ve “mastered the ladder.”

Why it Works:
It gamifies tempo training by giving structure and consequence. You learn to add speed without adding tension, the hallmark of players like Ernie Els, Adam Scott, and Tiger at his best.

title: Chipping Ladder Drill
description: Setup: Place 5 towels (or tees/hula hoops) in a line at 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 feet from your chipping spot. These are your landing zones, like rungs on a ladder. Execution: Starting at the closest target, chip one ball attempting to LAND it on or within 2 feet of the towel. Once you hit the first target, move to the second, then third, etc. If you miss a target, you must start over from the beginning. Rules: You must hit them in order (can't skip). Each ball must land on the target before you progress. This builds: (1) Distance control under pressure, (2) Focus on landing spot (not result), (3) Consistent technique regardless of distance. Adjust backswing length to change distance—not swing speed. Track how far up the ladder you can get. Goal: Complete all 5 rungs without restart.

title: Lead Arm Chipping Drill
description: Setup: Grip your wedge with ONLY your lead hand (left hand for right-handers). Place your trail hand behind your back or in your pocket. Address a ball with your normal chipping stance. Execution: Make chip shots using only your lead arm. This drill teaches: (1) Quiet wrists—you physically can't flip with one arm, (2) Pendulum motion controlled by shoulder rock, (3) Proper acceleration through the ball. Focus on your lead shoulder going down in the backswing and up in the follow-through, with the arm swinging as one unit. The ball should pop up softly with minimal effort. Start with very short chips (5-10 feet), then progress to longer ones. Hit 15-20 one-arm chips, then add trail hand and replicate the same stable-wrist, pendulum feel.

title: Use the Tee Wisely Drill
description: Tee the ball high for a draw or low for a fade. Adjust tee height and position to help shape your tee shots.

title: Fairway Finder Game
description: Set imaginary fairway boundaries on the range and challenge yourself to hit a certain number of drives within them; improves accuracy and pressure management.

title: Weight Transfer Heel Lift Drill
description: Lift your lead heel at the top of the backswing then plant it forcefully to start the downswing; this promotes proper weight transfer and power.

title: Shanks Game — Gate Outside the Ball
description: Set two tees just outside the ball forming a gate. Hit 15 shots without touching the tees. +1 per clean swing. Reset after any gate strike.

title: Head in a Box Throughout the Swing Feel
description: A common reason why you thin the ball is b/c you’re lifting your head too early. If you watch most pro golfers, the head actually bobs down first before it comes up. Feel like you’re keeping your head in a box throughout the swing and now allowing it to move out of it. Caution: don’t let yourself tighten or restrict your body from moving

title: Butt Back Posture Drill
description: Address a chair or wall behind you and maintain slight contact with your rear throughout the swing; ensures correct posture and prevents early extension.

title: Slice Fix Noodle Drill
description: Place a swimming noodle just outside the target line and swing to avoid hitting it; this encourages an inside-out swing path to eliminate slices.

title: Broom Chipping Drill
description: Setup: Grab a household broom (or mop) and hold it like a golf club in your chipping stance—hands on the stick, bristle end down. Execution: Make chipping motions with the broom, swinging it back and through toward an imaginary target. The long handle exaggerates any wrist breakdown—if you flip your wrists, the broom handle will hit your lead side. Key feels: (1) Keep your wrists quiet and firm throughout, (2) Rock your shoulders like a pendulum, (3) The butt of the broom should point at your belly button through the entire stroke. This teaches the 'putting stroke' style of chipping where the triangle formed by shoulders and arms stays intact. Practice 20-30 swings, then transfer the feel to actual chips with your wedge. The arms and club move as one unit.

title: Fat Game — Line-After-Ball Challenge
description: Draw a line 1 inch ahead of the ball. Hit 10 shots. +1 only if the first ground contact is on or after the line. Track streaks.

title: Extension & Rotation Drill #1
description: After impact, extend both arms and rotate your body toward the target; practise holding this extension to promote a full finish.

title: Mid‑Spine Rotation Feel
description: Place a club across your shoulders and rotate around your mid‑spine to feel the correct coil and avoid swaying.

title: Ball Position Adjustments Drill
description: Experiment with ball position (forward, middle, back) during practice to see how it influences contact and flight; teaches proper setup for each iron.

title: Dollar Signs Game
description: Setup: Around the practice green, place 5 dollar bills (or towels/tees) at different distances: 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 feet from your chipping spot. Each target represents a landing zone. Execution: Chip 3 balls to each target, trying to land directly on the dollar bill. Scoring: $5 for landing ON the bill, $2 for within 1 club length, $0 for missing. Total possible = $75. Track your score over multiple rounds. Key technique: Focus on your LANDING SPOT, not the hole—the ball's first bounce determines where it finishes. Control landing spot through club selection and backswing length. Use less loft for longer chips (PW), more loft for shorter (SW). Goal: Beat your previous score each session.

title: Throw the Basketball Down Feel
description: To combat coming across the ball, try to feel like you're holding a basketball and throwing it down right next to your right foot on the downswing

title: Anxiety Elimination Focus
description: Pick a spot a few inches in front of the ball and focus on that during your swing; focusing ahead instead of on impact reduces anxiety and tension.

title: Draw Game — 9-Ball Draw Window
description: Hit a 3‑ball set: low, mid, high draws that start right and finish at the target. Score +1 for each window you hit. Try to beat your best out of 9.

title: Ultimate Short Game Practice Challenge
description: Create rings at 3 and 6 feet around a hole and attempt chips from eight different lies (chip‑and‑run, pitches, flops, bunker shots). Score points based on landing inside the rings.

title: Takeaway Drill #2
description: Practise taking the club back until the shaft is parallel to the ground while keeping the clubface pointed slightly down; ensures proper wrist hinge and clubface control.

title: Stop Coming Over the Top Drill
description: Lift the club up above your head and practise swinging on a slightly flatter plane; encourages an inside path and prevents an over‑the‑top move.

title: Engage Your Legs Exercise
description: Perform half‑squat exercises and practise swinging while feeling tension in your quads; helps use the ground and engages your lower body.

title: Tee Outside The Ball Drill
description: Set a tee in the ground just outside the ball (heel side) by half an inch. Hit 20 shots avoiding the outside tee. If you strike the tee, reset and step back to slow down. Focus on brushing the ground slightly toe‑side. Track clean reps out of 20.

title: Master Your Downswing Drill
description: Setup: Take your normal stance with a mid-iron. Execution: Make a backswing and pause at the top. From the top, feel your weight shift to your lead foot FIRST while keeping your arms/hands back. Let your hips start rotating toward the target before your arms drop. Your hands should feel like they're falling straight down while your lower body leads. Hit balls focusing on this sequence: weight shift → hip rotation → arms drop → impact. Start with half swings at 50% speed until the sequence feels natural.

title: Fix Your Slice - Start With The Clubface
description: Fixing your slice starts with the clubface, not your path. Steps: (1) STRONGER GRIP: Rotate both hands clockwise on the grip until you see 2-3 knuckles on your lead hand. The V's formed by thumb/forefinger should point to your trail shoulder. (2) CHECK TAKEAWAY: When the club reaches waist height in your backswing, the clubface should match your spine angle—not point at the sky (open) or ground (closed). (3) FACE AWARENESS DRILL: Hit shots focusing ONLY on where the face points at impact. Try to hit hooks intentionally—if you can hit a hook, you can control the face. Practice: 10 shots with exaggerated strong grip, 10 with normal grip maintaining face awareness.

title: The Axe Drill - Fix Your Release
description: Setup: Hold a club with your normal grip, standing in your address position. Execution: Imagine you're holding an axe and about to chop into a tree at waist height on your lead side. Make swings focusing on driving the club DOWN and THROUGH like chopping wood—your hands should lead and the clubhead trails. The motion is a downward strike, not a scooping or flipping action. Feel your lead wrist stay flat or slightly bowed through impact while the trail wrist hinges back. Practice slow-motion swings first, then hit balls focusing on this chopping-down sensation through the ball.

title: Eliminate Casting Drill
description: Setup: Take your address position. Hold a water bottle or headcover against your trail hip with your trail elbow. Execution: Make swings keeping the object pinned to your hip as long as possible during the downswing. This forces your trail elbow to stay connected to your body rather than throwing out (casting). The elbow should only separate from your hip AFTER your hands pass your trail thigh. Feel: Your hands should lead the clubhead into impact—if you cast, the object will fall before you reach the ball. Practice drill: 10 swings at 50% speed keeping the object pinned, then 10 at 75%, then hit balls. Focus on maintaining the connection until you feel the natural release point.

title: Quickly Learn Course Management
description: Quick course management rules to apply immediately: (1) OFF THE TEE: Use the club that leaves you in the fairway, even if it's a 5-iron. Fairway > distance. (2) APPROACH SHOTS: Aim for the center of the green—pin hunting costs strokes. (3) CALCULATE MISS ZONES: Always pick a target where BOTH a pull and push still find the green/fairway. (4) TROUBLE SHOTS: Take your medicine—punch out sideways costs 1 stroke; hero shots often cost 3+. (5) SHORT GAME: Never short-side yourself—leave room for error on the safe side of the pin. (6) THINK BACKWARDS: Walk back from the green to plan each hole—what's your ideal approach distance? Apply one rule per round until automatic.

title: Hit Ball First Then Ground - Perfect Contact Drill
description: Peter Finch shows you how to hit the golf ball first then the ground for perfect contact every time. This drill addresses fat and thin shots by teaching proper low point control.

title: Basic Drill for Instant Compression
description: Setup: Address the ball with a 7-iron. Place your hands about 2 inches ahead of the ball (toward the target) so the shaft leans forward. Execution: Maintain this shaft lean throughout the swing and replicate it at impact—hands MUST be ahead of the clubhead when you strike the ball. Start with small punch shots (backswing to hip height, follow-through to hip height) focusing on keeping hands leading through impact. Gradually increase swing length while maintaining the 'hands ahead' impact position. Key checkpoint: At impact, you should feel like you're hitting down on the ball, with the club compressing the ball against the turf. Your divot should start AFTER the ball position.

title: The Plate Drill - Swing Path Fix
description: Setup: Visualize a dinner plate tilted at the same angle as your club shaft at address—roughly 45-60 degrees depending on the club. Execution: Your goal is to swing the club along this tilted plane, not vertically like chopping wood or horizontally like a baseball swing. On the backswing, feel the club travel up and around along this tilted plate. On the downswing, trace the same tilted circle back down. A helpful checkpoint: at waist height in the backswing, the club should point parallel to your target line, not at the sky or ground. Practice with half swings, ensuring the club stays on this imaginary tilted plate throughout.

title: Compression Drill - Dangerously Good Ball Striking
description: Setup: Place a tee in the ground about 4 inches in front of the ball on your target line. Use a 7 or 8-iron. Execution: Your goal is to hit the ball FIRST, then clip the tee out of the ground on the follow-through. This ensures you're striking down on the ball with forward shaft lean (hands ahead of clubhead at impact). Key feels: press your hands forward at address so the shaft leans toward the target; maintain this angle through impact; your divot should start AFTER the ball position. If you hit the tee before the ball or miss the tee entirely, you're scooping. Hit 20 balls focusing on ball-then-tee contact.

title: Putting Distance Control Drill
description: Setup: On the practice green, place 4 tees in a line at 15, 30, 45, and 60 feet from your starting position. Execution: Without aiming at a hole, putt one ball to each tee, trying to stop the ball as close to each tee as possible. Focus on FEEL, not mechanics—look at the tee, feel the distance, then stroke. The key is matching your backswing length to the distance: short backswing for short putts, longer for distance. Never change your tempo or hit harder—only change backswing length. Practice routine: Putt to each tee 3 times in a row, tracking how close you finish. Your goal is to get all putts within 3 feet of each tee. This builds your internal 'speedometer' for lag putting.

title: Perfect Weight Shift Drill
description: Setup: Take your normal stance. Place a golf ball or small object under the outside of your trail foot (right foot for righties). Execution: Make swings where you feel pressure move from the ball of your trail foot in the backswing to your lead foot in the downswing. By impact, 80%+ of your weight should be on your lead foot. The object under your trail foot gives instant feedback—if you hang back, you'll feel stuck on it. Key checkpoints: at the top of backswing, pressure is on the inside of your trail foot; by impact, your trail heel should be lifting off the ground. Practice 20 swings at half speed, then progress to full swings.

title: This Drill Makes Golf Easy
description: Setup: Take your normal stance with a 7-iron. Place a second ball about 12 inches in front of your ball on the target line. Execution: Your goal is to hit your ball, then continue through and roll the second ball forward with your follow-through. This promotes proper extension through the ball and prevents the common fault of 'quitting' at impact. The drill forces you to swing THROUGH the ball, not AT it. Key feels: keep accelerating through impact, let your arms extend toward the target, chest should face the target in your finish. If you miss the second ball, you're likely decelerating or flipping. Hit 20 balls focusing on ball-then-second-ball contact.

title: Rotation Drill for Backswing and Downswing
description: Setup: Take your stance and cross your arms over your chest, hands on opposite shoulders. Execution: Make a backswing by rotating your chest and shoulders while keeping your lower body stable—feel your lead shoulder turn under your chin. Your hips should only rotate about half as much as your shoulders (45° hips vs 90° shoulders). For the downswing, initiate by bumping your lead hip toward the target, then rotating your hips OPEN while keeping your chest back momentarily. This creates the 'X-factor stretch' that generates power. Practice 20 rotations without a club, then do 10 with a club across your shoulders, then hit balls.

title: The Drill That Fixes 90% of Amateur Swings
description: Setup: Place a headcover or small towel about 6 inches behind the ball, slightly inside your target line. Execution: Make swings WITHOUT hitting the headcover on the downswing. If you come over the top (the most common amateur fault), you'll hit the headcover. The correct move is to feel the club dropping DOWN and from the INSIDE on the downswing. Start with slow-motion practice swings, then progress to half-speed shots. Focus on keeping your back to the target longer in transition while letting the arms drop. Success = missing the headcover and hitting the ball with a slight draw.

title: 5 Simple Ways to Fix Your Hook
description: Rick Shiels guarantees these 5 simple fixes will cure your hook. Learn to weaken your grip, adjust your ball position, change your swing path, and stop the hands from rolling over too quickly at impact.

title: Best Way to Shallow the Club - Finally!
description: Setup: Take your address position with a mid-iron. Place an alignment stick or club on the ground pointing at your target. Execution: Make a backswing, then PAUSE at the top. From the pause, focus on two moves happening together: (1) your trail elbow drops straight down toward your trail hip, and (2) your hips begin rotating open. This combination 'shallows' the club onto the correct inside path. The club should feel like it's falling BEHIND you, not out toward the ball. Practice the pause-and-drop motion 10 times without a ball, then hit shots. The ball should start slightly right with a baby draw.

title: Effortless Golf Swing - Tempo Drill
description: Setup: Take your normal stance with a 7-iron. Execution: Count out loud 'one... two... three' as you swing. 'One' is at address, 'two' is at the top of your backswing, 'three' is at the finish. The key: spend the SAME amount of time going back (one to two) as you do going through (two to three). Most amateurs rush the downswing—this drill forces equal time back and through. Start with half swings at very slow speed, then gradually increase. Your arms and body should move together, not independently. Hit 10 balls counting out loud, then 10 counting silently. Ideal tempo is about 3:1 ratio (3 counts back, 1 count through) for full speed swings.

title: The Drill That Fixes 90% of Amateur Swings (Kerrod)
description: Setup: Take your address position with a mid-iron. Execution: Make swings focusing on RELEASING the club through impact, not dragging the handle. The key move: as you approach the ball, feel your trail forearm rotating over your lead forearm (like turning a doorknob counterclockwise for right-handers). The clubhead should pass your hands shortly after impact—NOT the hands staying ahead forever. Common amateur fault: 'holding off' the release, which leaves the face open and loses power. Key feels: (1) Let the clubhead 'throw' past your hands after impact, (2) Feel the toe of the club passing the heel through the hitting zone, (3) Your trail hand should feel like it's firing through, not being dragged. Practice: Make 10 slow-motion swings feeling the forearm rotation, then hit balls. The ball should start straight or with a slight draw. Goal: Eliminate the weak fade caused by holding off the release.

title: Effortless Golf Swing - Downswing Transition
description: Setup: Address the ball normally with a mid-iron. Execution: Make a backswing and pause for a full second at the top. From the pause, initiate the downswing by pressing your lead foot into the ground and letting your lead hip 'bump' toward the target about 2 inches. Your arms and club should stay back momentarily—they follow the lower body, not lead it. Feel: it's like your lower body starts walking toward the target while your upper body stays behind. This separation creates the 'effortless' power sensation. Practice sequence: 10 swings with a 2-second pause at top, then 10 with 1-second pause, then 10 continuous swings maintaining the same lower-body-first feel.

title: Easy Drill to Release the Club Perfectly
description: Setup: Hold the club in your lead hand only, at address position. Execution: Make slow swings with just your lead arm, focusing on rotating your forearm through impact so the toe of the club passes the heel (the club 'turns over'). Feel: your lead arm rotates like turning a doorknob counterclockwise (for right-handers). Now add your trail hand loosely and repeat—the trail hand supports but doesn't dominate. The release should feel like the club is 'free-wheeling' through impact, not held off or flipped. Checkpoint: at waist-high in your follow-through, the toe should point to the sky. Hit 10 balls with lead arm only, then 20 with both hands focusing on matching that release feel.

title: Best Rotation Drill to Get Open at Impact
description: Setup: Address the ball, then place a golf club or alignment stick across your hips (through your belt loops or held against your hip bones). Execution: Make swings focusing on getting the stick/club to point LEFT of target (for right-handers) at impact. At address, it points at the target. At impact, it should point 30-45° open (left). This requires your hips to rotate faster than your shoulders. Key feel: start the downswing by driving your lead hip back and around, not sliding toward the target. Your belt buckle should face the target or even left of target at impact. Practice 10 slow-motion swings checking hip position at impact, then hit balls focusing on this 'open hips' feel.

title: Improve Your Chipping Around the Green
description: Setup: Narrow stance, ball in the middle or slightly back. Press your hands forward so the shaft leans toward the target. Keep 60% weight on your lead foot. Execution: The chipping motion is a small version of your full swing—NOT a putting stroke. Let your wrists hinge slightly on the backswing, then unhinge naturally through impact. Key feel: your chest rotates through the shot (don't just use your arms). The club should bottom out AFTER the ball, taking a small divot. Distance control: vary backswing length, NOT hand speed. Short backswing = short chip. Practice hitting chips to specific targets at 10, 20, and 30 feet.

title: Must Use Short Game Drill - Proven Results
description: Setup: Around the practice green, place 5 balls at varying distances (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 feet) from a hole. Use one club for all shots (start with a 56° wedge). Execution: Chip each ball and note how close you finish. The goal is to get all 5 within a 3-foot circle of the hole. Key technique: Keep your weight 60% on your lead foot throughout, hands ahead of the clubhead at impact, and control distance with backswing length NOT hand speed. Repeat from different lies (uphill, downhill, tight, fluffy). Track your score over time—count how many finish inside 3 feet.

title: How to Start the Downswing - Simple Drill
description: Setup: Take your stance and make a backswing to the top. Pause. Execution: From the top, the FIRST move is a small lateral shift of your hips toward the target (about 2 inches)—feel like you're gently bumping your lead hip toward the target. THEN start rotating. This 'bump then turn' sequence is what the pros do. Common mistake: rotating immediately without the bump causes over-the-top. Practice drill: Make 10 backswings, pause at top, consciously bump lead hip, then rotate and swing through. The sequence should feel like: complete backswing → pause → hip bump → hip rotation → arms drop → release. Start at 50% speed.

title: The #1 Golf Chipping Method
description: Setup: Narrow stance (feet almost touching), ball position center or slightly back, weight 70% on lead foot. Open the clubface slightly at address. Execution: The 'chip and slide' technique uses the bounce of the club, not the leading edge. Press hands slightly forward, then make a short backswing hinging your wrists just slightly. On the downswing, feel like you're sliding the club UNDER the ball while the face stays open. The club should brush the grass, not dig. Key feels: keep your chest moving through the shot (don't stop at impact), let the loft do the work, and maintain the open face through impact. Practice with your 56° or 60° wedge from various lies.

title: Simple Drill for Perfect Golf Takeaway
description: Setup: Address the ball normally, then place a second ball (or tee) about 18 inches directly behind your clubhead on the target line. Execution: Start your backswing by pushing the clubhead straight back to knock away the second ball. This promotes a one-piece takeaway where your shoulders, arms, and club move together. Common faults this fixes: picking the club up too quickly, rolling the wrists open, or taking the club too far inside. Checkpoints: When the club reaches waist height, the toe should point to the sky and the shaft should be parallel to your target line. Practice 10-15 takeaways before hitting balls.

title: Stop Casting and Create Lag Drill
description: Setup: Hold the club with your normal grip and take your address position. Execution: Make a backswing to the top, then STOP. From here, focus on starting down by pulling your hands/grip straight DOWN toward the ground while keeping the clubhead UP and back. Feel like you're increasing the angle between your lead forearm and the club shaft (creating lag). The clubhead should feel like it's lagging way behind your hands. Only release this angle when your hands reach hip height. Practice in slow motion: backswing → pause → hands drop while clubhead stays back → release through impact. Hit balls at 50% speed until this feels natural.

title: Holy Grail of Course Management
description: Key principles for smarter course management: (1) AIM FOR THE FAT PART: Always aim at the widest part of the fairway/green, not the flag. (2) MISS IN THE RIGHT SPOT: Before each shot, identify where you can miss and still have an easy next shot—avoid short-sided chips. (3) TAKE YOUR MEDICINE: After a bad shot, prioritize getting back in play over hero recovery shots. (4) PLAY TO YOUR STRENGTHS: If you fade the ball, aim left and let it work right. (5) CLUB UP AND SWING EASY: One more club with a smooth swing beats forcing a shorter club. (6) LEAVE YOURSELF FULL SHOTS: Lay up to your favorite yardage, not as close as possible. Apply one principle per round until it becomes automatic.

title: The Last Putting Lesson You Need - 3 Simple Tips
description: Three fundamentals for better putting: (1) SETUP: Eyes directly over the ball (drop a ball from your eye line to check). Weight slightly favoring lead foot. Ball position just forward of center. Hands directly under shoulders. (2) STROKE PATH: The putter should swing like a pendulum from your shoulders—not your wrists. Place two tees just wider than your putter head and stroke between them without hitting. The putter face stays square to the arc. (3) DISTANCE CONTROL: Practice the 'ladder drill'—putt to 10, 20, 30 feet focusing only on distance, not direction. Match backswing length to distance; never change tempo. Practice each element for 5 minutes before playing.

title: Easy Way to Hole More Putts - Technique & Control
description: Setup: On the practice green, set up a putt of 6-10 feet. Place a tee in the ground 6 inches past the hole on your target line. Execution: Focus on rolling the ball at a speed that would get it to the tee if the hole wasn't there. This 'die speed' gives you the best chance of the ball catching the lip and falling in. For technique: keep your eyes over the ball, rock your shoulders like a pendulum (not your wrists), and let the putter head swing through naturally. Practice drill: Hit 10 putts trying to stop the ball between the hole and the tee. Track how many you make and how many finish in the 'golden zone' past the hole but short of the tee.

title: Downswing Drill for Contact & Accuracy
description: Setup: Take your address position and make a backswing to the top. Pause with club parallel to ground. Execution: From the top, focus on these three moves happening in sequence: (1) Lead hip bumps toward target, (2) Trail elbow drops down close to your trail hip, (3) Hands/club follow the elbow down. The club should feel like it's falling into the 'slot' behind you, not thrown out toward the ball. Key checkpoint: when your hands reach hip height, the club shaft should be pointing at or slightly right of your target—not at the ball. Practice: 10 slow-motion reps pausing at the top, 10 continuous swings at 50% speed, then gradually increase to full speed.

title: Easy Chip Shot Technique
description: Setup: Ball position slightly back of center, hands ahead of the ball, weight 60-70% on your lead foot. Shaft should lean toward the target. Execution: Use a narrow stance (feet about 6 inches apart). Keep your weight on your lead foot throughout—don't shift back. Make a short backswing using mostly arm swing with minimal wrist hinge. Stroke THROUGH the ball with a descending blow, feeling like you're brushing the grass after the ball. The clubhead never passes your hands until well after impact. Think 'pendulum' with your arms while your body stays quiet. Start with a pitching wedge for bump-and-runs before progressing to lofted wedges.

title: Hit Every Club Longer - Distance Drill
description: An incredible drill to add distance to every club in your bag. Learn to generate more clubhead speed through proper sequencing and efficient energy transfer from the ground up.

title: 5 Easy Ways to Stop Your Slice
description: Five fixes to eliminate your slice: (1) GRIP: Strengthen your grip by rotating both hands clockwise on the club until you see 3 knuckles on your lead hand. (2) CLUB FACE: Practice closing the face at address slightly—aim the face where you want the ball to START. (3) TAKEAWAY: On the backswing, keep the clubface pointing at the ball longer; don't roll it open. (4) PATH: Spray foot powder on your clubface and hit a ball—the mark shows your actual path. Gear marks toward the heel = over the top. (5) RELEASE: Feel like you're turning the club face over through impact, like turning a doorknob counterclockwise. Practice each fix separately before combining them.

title: Dead Hand Chipping
description: Keep your hands completely passive—"dead"—throughout the chip shot. No wrist hinge on the backswing, no flipping through impact. Your shoulders and arms control the motion like a pendulum, while your hands simply hold on for the ride. Day uses this to eliminate the yips and produce ultra-consistent contact. The key: if your hands feel like they're doing nothing, you're doing it right.

title: Weight Forward
description: Keep your weight forward onto your lead foot as you are chipping. Unlike iron shots we don’t want to worry about timing the weight transfer.

title: Toe Down Chipping
description: When chipping keep an upright handle with the toe down which helps to avoid contact with the ground so this is great for uncomfortable and tight lies. A great feel for winter golf or Texas hardpan.

title: Ear to the Ground
description: Forget 'keep your head down'—it kills rotation. Instead, let your head turn naturally through impact so your trail ear rotates toward the ground. This frees your body to rotate fully through the shot rather than stalling with a locked head position. Rose uses this feel to ensure his chest and hips can clear without restriction. If you're blocking shots or losing power, a fixed head is often the culprit.

title: Simon Says Game
description: A reactive game that tests adaptability under pressure. Stand behind your opponent and call out a shot type (draw, punch, high fade) as they begin their takeaway. If they pull off the called shot, they earn a point. Failed attempts score nothing. First to 5 points wins. Warning: this game involves talking during someone's backswing.

title: HORSE
description: Bring the classic basketball game to the range. Take turns calling and executing specific shots (e.g., 'land within 10 yards of the 150-yard marker'). If you make it, your opponent must match it. If they fail, they earn a letter. First to spell H-O-R-S-E loses. Variation: allow one mulligan per shot to keep things friendly.

title: Stomp Drill (Tommy Fleetwood)
description: In your backswing, lift your lead foot completely off the ground. As you start the downswing, stomp or step that foot back down toward the target before striking the ball. This forces proper weight transfer and prevents hanging back—one of the main causes of skulls and shanks. Many tour players use this on the range. The stomp gives you insurance against falling onto your back foot. Practice 15-20 shots exaggerating the step until forward weight shift feels automatic.

title: Squat and Turn
description: At the top of your backswing, focus on pushing down and back with the butt to start the downswing. Feel like you are squatting and turning through the shot. This prevents early extension and keeps the club from getting stuck behind you, promoting better sequencing through impact.

title: Hip Space Drill (Scottie Scheffler)
description: Place a pencil or tee just outside the butt end of your grip at address. Make swings keeping your hips and pelvis back throughout—creating space for the club handle to return to its original position at impact. Scheffler's elite ball striking comes from maintaining this space rather than thrusting his hips toward the ball. If you lose the space, you'll hit the pencil. This promotes clean, powerful contact by keeping your body organized through the hitting zone. Practice slow-motion swings feeling your hips stay back while your arms deliver the club.

title: Guide Trail Elbow Feel
description: Rose's downswing secret is keeping the trail elbow in front of the body rather than letting it flare behind you. When the right arm gets 'disconnected' and works too far behind in the backswing, it's nearly impossible to shallow the club. The fix: feel like you keep your trail elbow pointing down and in front of your chest throughout the swing. This prevents the arm from getting deep behind you and naturally gets the shaft to lay down in transition. Practice by placing your trail arm across your chest at address, feeling how it stays connected. Then make swings focusing on that elbow staying forward—never letting it work behind your torso. The result is effortless shallowing and a powerful inside path.

title: Skip a Rock
description: If your upper body spins open too early in the downswing, you'll come over the top and lose power. Rose's fix: think of skimming a rock across water. When you skip a stone, your body stays back while your arm whips through—if you spin your chest toward the target too soon, the rock goes straight into the water. Apply the same feeling to your swing: at the top, keep your chest closed while your arms drop and hips begin to clear. The upper body 'waits' while the lower body leads. Practice slow-motion swings exaggerating this separation—feel like you're skimming a rock with your trail arm while your chest stays back. When you finally rotate through, the club attacks from the inside with effortless speed.

title: Windmill Drill (Tommy Fleetwood)
description: Make half swings with straight arms—no wrist hinge, no hand manipulation. Your body rotation alone moves the club. Fleetwood calls these 'windmill swings' because your arms stay extended like windmill blades while your torso turns. This drill re-establishes connection between arms and body when you're getting stuck or hooking. Fleetwood worked on this for six months when rebuilding his swing. Hit 20 half-shots focusing purely on body turn, then gradually add wrist hinge back in.

title: Split-Hands Drill (Rory McIlroy)
description: Grip the club normally with your lead hand but place your trail hand at the very bottom of the grip, leaving a gap between hands. Make swings with the goal of getting both arms straight as soon as possible in the downswing. This forces your trail arm to straighten and compress the ball while your chest rotates toward the target at impact. It's straight from the Pete Cowen school—using your arms to apply pressure onto the ball rather than flipping. Hit 15-20 balls feeling the trail arm extend through impact.

title: Hands to Pocket Feel
description: From the top of your backswing, feel like your hands drop straight into your back pocket as you rotate through. This promotes natural shallowing—the club approaches from inside without manipulation. To rehearse, start at the top and move at 40% speed, dropping hands to your rear pocket and holding that position. The motion prevents coming over the top and encourages an inside path. Bryson says this one feel, done correctly, fixes the steep swing that causes slices and weak contact.

title: Hip Drop Power Move (Tiger Woods)
description: On the backswing, feel your trail hip (right glute) drop slightly lower to the ground rather than spinning level. You'll know it's working when your trail glute feels tight and loaded—it's a monster power move. This was Tiger's key swing thought that helped him win the 2019 Masters. The lower trail hip creates torque and takes pressure off your spine for pain-free rotation. As you start down, that stored energy releases explosively. Practice feeling the right hip 'sit' on the backswing before firing through.

title: Hip Height Power Drill (Jon Rahm)
description: Grab a 6-iron and swing back only until your hands reach hip height, then hit the shot at full speed. This abbreviated backswing forces you to generate power with your lower body instead of your arms—creating a whip-like action through impact. Rahm says if you don't use your hips, there's no power in the swing. The drill teaches the disassociation between lower and upper body that creates effortless speed. Do 10 reps, focusing on firing your hips hard from a shorter backswing.

title: Dead Hand Wedge Feel (Jason Day)
description: Keep your hands completely passive—'dead'—throughout the wedge shot. No wrist hinge, no manipulation, no flipping. Your body rotation and shoulder turn control the motion while your hands simply maintain their position on the grip. This promotes consistent contact and distance control on pitch shots and chips. Day's key: the quieter your hands, the more reliable your short game.

title: Three-Foot Circle Game (Phil Mickelson)
description: Whether chipping or putting, your only goal is getting the ball inside a three-foot circle around the hole. Phil calls this the 'foundation' of his entire short game. For practice, set up 10 balls around a hole with some break and try to make 100 three-footers in a row. This shifts your focus from making everything to leaving tap-ins—which is what actually saves strokes. The mental freedom of aiming for a zone rather than the hole reduces tension and produces better distance control.

title: Feel vs. Real: Drop the Arms
description: At the top of your backswing, pause and let your arms drop straight down toward your trail thigh while keeping your chest closed—don't rotate yet. The club will feel like it's falling way behind you. Once your hands reach thigh height, rotate hard through to finish. This exaggerated "inside drop" feels wrong but produces a neutral path when you add rotation. Rose calls it the boat and water skier: as the boat (you) turns, the skier (club) gets thrown out.

title: Short Putt Routine
description: Rose's short putt routine is deliberately minimal: one shoulder-driven practice stroke to feel tempo, step in, set the face first where you want the ball to start, then set your feet, and go. No extra waggles or looks—once set, commit and stroke. The entire sequence should take 8-10 seconds max. By keeping it short and identical every time, you eliminate overthinking under pressure.

title: Line Strike Consistency Test (Bryson DeChambeau)
description: Draw a line on a mat or in the sand where the ball would be. Practice hitting that line with your club's low point—just after where the ball sits. Bryson's benchmarks: hit the line 5 times in a row for 10-handicap consistency, 10-12 times for scratch, 20+ times for tour-level. This drill reveals the truth about your ball striking—if you can't consistently bottom out in the same spot, nothing else matters. It's the foundation of compression and clean contact.

title: Nine Windows
description: Tiger's famous warm-up drill for complete ball flight control. Hit 9 different shots in sequence: draw, straight, fade, low draw, low straight, low fade, high draw, high straight, and high fade. Ideally complete in 9 balls, but 18-27 is realistic for most golfers. Competitive version: each player gets 9 balls, most successful shots wins.

title: Play “a Round” on the Range
description: Escape range monotony by visualizing actual holes. Picture a course that you’ve played before and cycle through all the shots you would need to make on each hole. Go through your pre-shot routine on every shot in order to simulate the feel of playing a round. Track your score for front, back, or full 18.

title: Shallow is Not Laying Down (Kawaswing)
description: The most common shallowing mistake is trying to 'lay the club down' or force it flat in transition. Kawaswing teaches that true shallowing happens through proper sequencing—not manipulation. Start the downswing with your lower body while your arms stay passive; the club will shallow naturally as it drops into the slot. If you actively try to flatten the shaft, you'll lose lag and come in too shallow with an open face. Let gravity and rotation do the work.

title: Butterfly Grip (Kawaswing)
description: Kawaswing's signature grip technique emphasizes a lighter, more neutral hold that promotes wrist hinge and club release. Rather than squeezing tightly, let the club sit in your fingers with a 'butterfly' lightness—firm enough to control but soft enough to allow natural wrist action. This reduces tension in the forearms and shoulders, enabling a freer swing with better lag retention and a more natural release through impact.

title: Hinge and Hold
description: For chip shots, hinge your wrists immediately on the takeaway, then HOLD that angle through impact—never release or flip. Phil says this is the only effective way to chip. Using a 60-degree wedge, break your wrists going back, lock them in that hinged position, then accelerate through the ball using shoulder rotation. The club stays ahead of your hands. This removes the timing issue of trying to release at the right moment and produces crisp, consistent contact. To hit it farther, simply lengthen your backswing while maintaining the same hinge-and-hold mechanics.

title: Belt Buckle Drill (Rory McIlroy)
description: Use your belt buckle as a rotation guide. Feel like your belt buckle faces the target at impact—not after, AT impact. This produces more hip rotation, more speed, and more consistent strikes. To practice, exaggerate intentionally turning your belt buckle toward the target during swings until the motion blends naturally. Rory says this one thought alone can unlock significant clubhead speed because it forces your body to clear rather than stall.

title: Right Side Bend for Impact (Kawaswing)
description: Leaning your upper body toward the target (right side bend for right-handers) is essential for solid impact. Kawaswing emphasizes that this forward lean isn't a sway—your head stays behind the ball while your spine tilts toward the target. This creates room for your arms to swing through and ensures you compress the ball with a descending blow. Practice by feeling your trail shoulder work down and under through impact rather than spinning level.

title: Pause at the Top Feel (Adam Scott)
description: Under pressure, give yourself a slight pause at the top of your backswing. This allows the club to 'find its slot' and transition naturally into the downswing rather than rushing. Adam Scott relies on this when he needs to find a fairway in a pressure moment—he reminds himself to swing smooth and let the transition happen naturally. The pause prevents the quick, jerky moves that destroy tempo when nerves kick in. Think 'one' on the backswing, brief pause, then 'two' at the ball.

title: Sternum Rotation Feel (Tiger Woods)
description: Start your backswing by rotating your sternum and ribcage—not by moving your hands. Place your trail hand on your sternum and feel it turn away from the target while your lead arm stays connected. What looks like Tiger starting with his hands is actually his upper body initiating the takeaway. This creates width, keeps you connected, and prevents the lifting or snatching move that throws off your plane. Practice 10 slow-motion takeaways feeling the sternum lead the movement.

title: Stop Topping Drill
description: Practise hitting down on the ball by focusing on keeping your head slightly behind the ball and extending your arms through impact; prevents topping or thinning.

title: Slice Game — Fairway Start Line Ladder
description: Pick a target line and set three cones progressively more right. Hit 5 drives trying to start between cone 1 and the target, then cone 2, then cone 3 without curving left.

title: Gate Putting Drill
description: Setup: Place two tees in the ground creating a 'gate' just slightly wider than your putter head (about 1/4 inch clearance on each side). Position the gate about 6 inches in front of your ball on your target line. Execution: Make putting strokes, rolling the ball through the gate without hitting either tee. Hitting a tee means your face angle or path is off. Start with 3-foot putts. Key technique: Focus on keeping the putter face square through impact and maintaining a straight-back, straight-through path (for short putts). Your eyes should stay over the ball, and the stroke should be a smooth pendulum. Success metric: Make 10 putts in a row through the gate. Once achieved, narrow the gate by 1/8 inch and repeat. This drill builds a repeatable stroke with consistent face angle.

title: Made in the Shade Bunker Drill
description: Hold an umbrella or alignment stick vertically above the ball and swing while keeping the clubface under the shade; encourages proper wrist hinge and shallow splash.

title: One-Handed Chipping Drill
description: Setup: Grip your wedge with ONLY your lead hand (left hand for righties). Use a pitching wedge or sand wedge. Position the ball slightly back of center, with your weight 60% on your lead foot. Execution: Make chip shots using only your lead hand/arm. Because you have no trail hand to 'help,' you MUST use body rotation to move the club—your shoulders rock like a pendulum while your wrist stays firm. The club should feel like an extension of your lead arm. Key benefits: (1) Eliminates the 'flipping' action that causes chunks and skulls, (2) Forces proper body rotation, (3) Trains the feeling of the lead arm controlling the stroke. Start with tiny chips (5-10 feet) and gradually increase distance. After 10 one-handed chips, add your trail hand back and try to replicate the same connected, body-controlled feeling. Goal: Hit 10 clean chips in a row with lead hand only.

title: Push Turn & Extend Drill
description: Push your lead arm straight at the start of the downswing while turning your body and extending through impact; encourages proper extension and rotation.

title: Topping Fix Resistance Band Drill
description: Secure a resistance band around both forearms and make swings; the band encourages your arms to stay connected and prevents early extension, curing topped shots.

title: Chipping Feel — Soft Wrists, Pivot Thru
description: Feel soft wrists with the chest turning through so the loft delivers the strike. No stab. Brush the grass.

title: Stamp Weight Shift Drill
description: Make practice swings lifting your lead heel and then stamp it down to start the downswing; this cues the correct weight transfer and dynamic pressure shift.

title: Tee Height Experiment Drill
description: Practise hitting irons off tees at different heights to see how contact and launch change; use this feedback to set tee height when using hybrids and fairway woods.

title: Pump the Club Twice Drill
description: "Pumping the club" in golf is a downswing drill that helps golfers achieve a better impact position by teaching them to initiate the downswing with their body rotation and downward movement of the arms, rather than an aggressive over-the-top chop. The drill involves going to the top of the backswing and performing a couple of short, controlled downward movements with the arms, simulating the correct body-to-club sequencing, before hitting the ball. This technique helps to shallow the club's path, control the clubface, prevent slicing, and improve contact with the ball.

title: Impact Drill #2
description: Setup: Place a folded towel or headcover about 4-5 inches BEHIND your ball (away from target). Use a 7-iron. Execution: Make swings hitting the ball cleanly WITHOUT hitting the towel on your backswing or downswing. If you hit the towel, you're either: (1) taking the club back too far inside, or (2) casting/releasing early on the downswing causing a fat shot. This drill promotes: a proper takeaway path, a descending strike (hitting ball first), and forward shaft lean at impact. Key checkpoint: Your low point should be AFTER the ball, not before it. The towel prevents scooping or hitting behind the ball. Start with half swings, then progress to full swings. Hit 20 balls tracking how many times you miss the towel completely.

title: Coin Putting Progression Drill
description: Set a coin on the carpet and practise rolling the ball over it from varying distances; start short and gradually move back to improve accuracy and pace control.

title: Pencil Face Control Drill
description: Setup: Using elastic bands, attach a pencil lengthwise to the back of your clubface so it extends outward like an antenna. Use a 7-iron. Execution: Make half-swing chip shots (waist-high to waist-high). Watch where the pencil points at impact and in your follow-through. If the pencil points LEFT of target at impact, your face is closed. If it points RIGHT, your face is open. For a square face, the pencil should point at your target through the hitting zone. Key feel: Focus on keeping the pencil pointing at your target as long as possible through impact. Practice 20 shots, adjusting your grip pressure and forearm rotation until the pencil consistently tracks toward target. Goal: Develop awareness of clubface orientation without relying on ball flight.

title: Sequencing Step Drill
description: Setup: Address the ball with your feet completely together (touching). Use a 7-iron. Execution: Make a full backswing with feet together. As you START the downswing, step your lead foot toward the target (about 6-8 inches) before striking the ball. The sequence is: backswing with feet together → lead foot steps toward target → then hit the ball. This drill forces proper weight transfer and sequencing—your lower body MUST lead because you're literally stepping first. Benefits: Prevents hanging back, promotes proper weight shift, and trains the feeling of lower body leading the downswing. Start with half swings at slow speed, then progress to full swings. Hit 20 balls focusing on the step timing.

title: 3-Ball Distance Control Putting Drill
description: Place three balls at increasing distances from the hole and try to lag each putt to stop within a grip-length of the hole; enhances distance control.

title: Spine Angle Check
description: Use a mirror or alignment stick to monitor your spine angle at setup and throughout the swing; maintaining the angle helps with consistent ball striking.

title: Shanks Feel — Handle High, Weight Left
description: Feel the handle a touch higher at address and a smidge more weight on the lead foot, then keep the handle away from the thigh in transition.

title: Swing to Right Field Feel (Exaggerated)
description: Feel like you’re swinging the club out to right field. Exaggerate the inside-out path to counter an over-the-top move.

title: Feet Together Drill
description: Setup: Address the ball with your feet touching (completely together). Use a 7-iron. Execution: Make smooth, controlled swings hitting balls with your feet together throughout. Because your base is narrow, you CANNOT make big weight shifts or aggressive moves—the drill forces you to swing with balance, tempo, and arm/body connection. If you swing too hard or lose your balance, you'll fall over. Key benefits: (1) Eliminates swaying and sliding, (2) Promotes connected arm swing with body rotation, (3) Forces smooth tempo, (4) Reveals if you're using too much arms vs body. Start with half swings at 50% power. Progress to 3/4 swings. You should be able to hold your finish perfectly balanced. Hit 20 balls; if you lose balance, slow down.

title: Fade and Draw Game
description: Hit one fade with your driver then hit a draw. For a fade think about coming over the top a bit. Make sure your alignment is right, open the shoulders hips and stance a bit. Draw - feel like you’re coming a hair inside to out. Close the shoulders, hips & stance. See how many in a row you can get alternating.

title: Ball-Striking Spray Drill
description: Spray a dry shampoo or foot spray on the clubface and hit shots to see where the ball contacts the face; aim to strike the middle for consistent ball striking.

title: Open Palm Swing Drill (Ludvig Aberg)
description: If you’re a right handed golfer, hold the club in your left hand and your right hand palm against the grip. Improves lag, reduces overswinging, keeps from coming over the top

title: Putting Gate Drill (Voice Caddie)
description: Setup: Place two tees in the ground about 3-4 feet in front of your ball, creating a 'gate' that's just slightly wider than your putter head (about 1/4 inch clearance on each side). Execution: Stroke putts through the gate without hitting either tee. Hitting the tees means your putter path or face angle is off. Key checkpoints: (1) If you hit the inside tee (closer to you), your path is too inside-out. (2) If you hit the outside tee, your path is too outside-in. (3) A square path goes straight through. Practice: Start with 3-foot putts through the gate. When you can make 10 in a row without hitting tees, move the gate closer to the ball (more challenging) or widen your stance. This drill trains consistent path and square face at impact.

title: Throw the Basketball Down Feel
description: To combat coming across the ball and swiping at it, try to feel like you’re holding a basketball and throwing it down right next to your right foot on the downswing. This forces you to drop your hands and keep your arms in front of the body

title: Fat Feel — Belt Buckle to Target
description: Feel the belt buckle pointing at the target at impact so the low point shifts forward and contact happens after the ball.

title: Up and Down Game
description:
On the short game practice area take one ball and chip then putt for 18 holes. This is meant to simulate the pressure of getting up and down over a round of golf where you only have one go at each hole in comparrison to repetivie practice. 
Scoring: 
-Chip in = -1
-Up and down = 0
-3 stroke = +1, 4 stroke = +2, etc 
Record your 18 hole score, lower the better!

title: Slice Drill — Alignment Stick Gate
description: Place two alignment sticks just wider than your clubhead angled slightly right of target. Make swings starting inside the gate and exiting right to promote an in-to-out path.

title: Accelerate Through Feel
description: Thin or chunk while chipping? Often times it’s b/c you’re trying to control distance by slowing down your swing, throwing off timing. Control distance with your backswing and accelerate through the shot and commit.

title: Left Hand Only Swing Drill
description: Make practice swings and even hit balls using only your left hand; trains your lead side to control the swing and prevents an over‑active right hand.

title: Cover the Ball Feel
description: Feel like your chest is covering the ball on the downswing. This helps if you have a tendency to flip or stand up. Fixes early extension

title: 10 Chips to a Towel Game
description: Put down a small towel and try and hit 10 chips to it. This helps you figure out distance & control. Use different wedges and different height shots

title: Alter Trajectory Drill
description: Setup: Use a 7-iron and hit three sets of shots to learn trajectory control. Execution: (1) LOW SHOT: Ball position back of center (off trail foot), weight 60% forward, hands well ahead, make a 3/4 punch swing with an abbreviated follow-through. (2) MEDIUM SHOT: Ball position center, weight 50/50, normal swing. (3) HIGH SHOT: Ball position forward (off lead foot), weight slightly back at address, feel like you're staying behind the ball and sweeping up through impact, full follow-through. Practice: Hit 5 balls at each trajectory consecutively, then randomize. Watch how the ball flights differ with the same club. This skill is essential for: playing in wind, hitting under trees, attacking pins. Goal: Be able to hit all 3 trajectories on command.

title: Club Starts at Parallel Feel
description: If you take the club too inside on the way back, you’ll want to come over the top causing a slice or hook. Bring the club to parallel, finish your back swing then swing through to feel what on plane feels like.

title: Pitching Swing Plane Drill
description: Setup: Lay two alignment sticks on the ground in a V-shape, creating a channel that narrows toward the target at roughly 45° angles. The narrow end should be about 6 inches wide (just wider than your club). Place your ball in the channel. Execution: Make pitch shots swinging your wedge through the channel without hitting either stick. This grooves an on-plane swing path. If you hit the inside stick: you're swinging too far inside. If you hit the outside stick: you're coming over the top. Key technique: The club should travel along the channel on both backswing and downswing. Start with short pitch shots and progress to longer ones. This drill eliminates the two main short game killers: chunking (too steep) and blading (too shallow). Hit 15-20 balls through the channel.

title: Draw Drill — Face-to-path stick drill
description: Setup: Place two alignment sticks on the ground. Stick #1 (body line): Aim 10-20 yards RIGHT of your target—this is your swing path line. Stick #2 (target line): Point directly at your target. Stand parallel to stick #1, so your feet, hips, and shoulders aim right of target. Ball position is normal (center for irons). Execution: Swing along your BODY line (stick #1), NOT at the target. Your club path will travel inside-to-out. Meanwhile, keep your clubface pointing at the actual TARGET (stick #2) at impact—slightly CLOSED relative to your swing path. This face-to-path relationship (closed face to in-to-out path) creates draw spin. Key feel: Swing 'out to right field' while the face looks at the target. Start with half swings, then progress to full shots. The ball should start right of target and curve back left. Goal: Hit 5 consecutive draws that start right and curve back to target.

title: Speed Ladder Putting Drill
description: Place tees or coins at three, six and nine feet and attempt to roll putts that finish just beyond each marker; helps develop feel for different distances.

title: Towel Chipping Setup Drill
description: Lay a towel on the floor and chip balls so they land on it; vary distances and clubs to learn how far chips carry and release.

title: Right forefinger/thumb off club
description: Your right elbow should naturally fold and not flare out. Take the tension out of your arm by taking your right forefinger and thumb off the club.

title: Pause at the Top Feel
description: Think Hideki or Cam Young. Pause at the top helps with tempo and allows the club a second to drop into the slot. Feel like you’re taking a 2 second pause at the top. If you film yourself doing this, you’ll be surprised to see there’s little to no pause… feel vs. real.

title: Takeaway Drill #1
description: Focus on keeping the clubhead low to the ground for the first few inches of the takeaway; this promotes a smooth one‑piece takeaway.

title: Wall Putting Stroke Drill
description: Stand with your backside against a wall and make putting strokes, ensuring the putter swings like a pendulum without your hips moving; promotes a rock-the-shoulders stroke.

title: Stay Closed to the Target
description: Feel like you are keeping your upper body closed to the target as you swing in order to promote and in to out swing path and avoid the dreaded slice.

title: Small Ball Between Forearms Drill
description: To keep the right elbow from flaring, try and swing with a small ball wedged between your forearms. This keeps your swing compact and connected

title: Par 18 Chipping Drill
description: Setup: Around the practice green, create 9 'holes' by selecting 9 different chip shot locations with varying distances, lies, and obstacles. Each location is one hole. Par for each hole = 2 (chip + putt). Execution: Play all 9 holes using one ball. Chip from each location, then putt out. Track your total strokes. Par = 18. Scoring: Under 18 = great day. 18-20 = solid. 21+ = needs work. Rules: You must play each chip where it lands (no mulligans). Vary the challenge: include uphill chips, downhill chips, over bunkers, tight lies, fluffy lies, etc. This game builds pressure and simulates real on-course scenarios. Track your Par 18 score over multiple sessions to measure improvement. Goal: consistently score 18 or better.

title: Tiger Woods Pause Drill
description: The Tiger Woods pause drill is a range staple for developing better tempo and transition control. Start by taking your normal backswing, then pause for a full second at the top—just long enough to feel the club settle and your lower body start to lead. From there, swing down smoothly without rushing, focusing on staying balanced and letting the sequence unfold naturally. Tiger has said he hated how uncomfortable this drill felt, but he credits it with sharpening his transition and helping him control the club under pressure.

title: Transition Drill #1
description: From the top of the backswing, initiate the downswing by shifting your weight to the lead foot before the arms drop; promotes proper sequencing.

title: Shank Buster Drill
description: Setup: Place a headcover, towel, or small box about 1 inch outside the TOE of your club at address (on the far side from you). Use a 7 or 8-iron. Execution: Make swings hitting the ball without touching the headcover. If you shank (hit the hosel), you'll strike the headcover. This drill works because shanks happen when the club moves OUT toward the ball during the downswing. The headcover forces you to swing more from the inside and make contact on the center or toe of the face. Key feels: (1) Feel like you're swinging the club more around your body, not out at the ball. (2) Try to hit the ball slightly toward the toe. (3) Keep your weight centered—don't lunge toward the ball. Hit 20 balls; if you hit the headcover, pause and reset.

title: H‑O‑R‑S‑E Driving Range Game
description: With a partner, call a shot shape or target and try to execute it; if your partner fails, they receive a letter. Continue until someone spells HORSE.

title: Accelerate Through the Swing Feel
description: Feel like you’re taking a shorter backswing but fully accelerating through the ball. It’s common to start guiding/flipping at the ball when you decelerate through the shot, resulting in a chunk or a thin

title: Clock Putting Drill
description: Setup: Place 12 balls around the hole at 3-foot distance, positioned like numbers on a clock (12, 1, 2, 3... etc.). Execution: Starting at 12 o'clock, attempt to make all 12 putts consecutively without missing. Rules: If you miss ANY putt, you must start over from 12 o'clock. This builds pressure and focus—as you progress around the clock, the stakes increase. Key technique: Read each putt properly (some will break left, some right, some straight), commit to your line, and stroke with confidence. Variations: (1) Beginner: Miss = restart from current position. (2) Advanced: Miss = restart from beginning. (3) Pro: Complete 2 full rotations (24 putts) without missing. Track your best streak.

title: Heel Away Feel
description: At address, feel the clubhead slightly more toe‑up and the handle a touch closer to the thigh. During the downswing, feel the hands in tight to the body while the clubhead works slightly out. This promotes a more toe‑side strike and moves the path away from the heel to reduce shanks.

title: Pencil & Coin Drill
description: Setup: Balance a pencil horizontally across the back of your putter head (in the cavity or along the back edge). Place a coin about 2 inches in front of your ball on your target line. Execution: Make putting strokes where you (1) keep the pencil balanced throughout the stroke (no wobble = stable putter face), and (2) roll the ball over the coin toward the hole. If the pencil falls, your stroke is too jerky or you're manipulating the face. If you miss the coin, your path is off. This drill trains: stable face angle, centered strike, and consistent path. Start with 3-foot putts, progress to 6 feet. Goal: 10 putts in a row keeping the pencil balanced and hitting the coin.

title: Shanks Drill — Toe-Strike Calibration
description: Place a tee just outside the ball. Intend to hit slightly off the toe. Film one swing to confirm path from the inside and toe‑side contact.

title: Transition Drill #2
description: Practise a slight bump of the hips toward the target before rotating; this lateral move triggers the downswing and encourages an inside path.

title: Tempo Game — Tempo Ladder
description: Climb 30‑50‑70‑90‑100% effort keeping the same rhythm. +1 for a clean climb without a rushed shot. Bonus for climb + descent.

title: Short Backswing Feel
description: All sorts of bad can happen when you overswing or have a long backswing. To work on a short compact swing, hit balls where you feel like you’re taking the club back halfway, a quick pause then swing all the way through and hold the finish through

title: Roll the Battery Drill
description: Setup: Place a AA or D battery on its side on the practice green (on a flat area). Address the battery with your putter as if it were a ball. Execution: Make putting strokes attempting to roll the battery in a straight line without it wobbling or veering off course. A wobbling battery indicates: (1) off-center contact, (2) an open or closed face at impact, or (3) an inconsistent stroke path. The battery amplifies any stroke flaws because it's more sensitive than a golf ball. Key focus: Strike the battery dead center with a square face and smooth acceleration. Practice until you can roll the battery 3-4 feet in a perfectly straight line consistently. Then transfer this centered, square stroke to actual putts.

title: One Shot, Three Clubs Game
description: Choose one location and hit the same chip shot using three different clubs (e.g., 7-iron, pitching wedge, lob wedge); improves creativity and adaptability.

title: 5 Ball Up-and-Down Challenge
description: Drop five balls around the green and attempt to get up-and-down with each; if you miss any up-and-down, restart the challenge until you complete all five.

title: Heads Up Putting Drill
description: Setup: On the practice green, set up putts of varying lengths (10, 20, 30, 40 feet). Execution: Instead of looking at the ball during your stroke, look at the HOLE throughout the entire stroke. Take your stance, look at the hole, and putt while keeping your eyes fixed on the hole. Benefits: (1) Improves distance control by engaging your natural depth perception, (2) Reduces putter face manipulation (you can't steer if you're not looking), (3) Builds trust in your stroke. This feels strange at first but many tour pros practice this way. Start with longer putts where speed matters more than line. Key: Your peripheral vision will still see the ball—trust it. Hit 20 putts 'eyes on hole' then compare your distance control to normal putting.

title: Connect the Lines Bunker Drill
description: Draw two parallel lines in the sand: one for where the club enters and one for where it exits. Swing so that the club enters the sand at the first line and exits at the second.

title: Pressure Putting Routine
description: Set up a circle of five 3-foot putts around the hole and try to make all five in a row; if you miss one, start over. Builds confidence under pressure.

title: Aim Small, Miss Small Feel
description: Pick a small target in the distance, such as a leaf or a branch, and focus on hitting it; improves focus and alignment.

title: Extension & Rotation Drill #2
description: Swing through and hold a balanced finish with your chest facing the target; this reinforces proper rotation and balance.

title: Tee Peg Pitching Drill
description: Setup: Place a ball on a low tee (about 1/2 inch high) as if teeing up a drive, but use your pitching wedge or sand wedge. Execution: Make pitch shots focusing on clipping the ball cleanly off the tee WITHOUT touching the ground or taking a divot. The tee should remain standing after impact. This drill trains: (1) proper low point control, (2) using the bounce of the club instead of digging with the leading edge, (3) crisp ball-first contact. Key technique: Keep your weight slightly forward, hands ahead of the ball, and make a smooth accelerating motion through impact. Don't try to help the ball up—let the loft do the work. Hit 20 balls; goal is 15+ clean picks off the tee.

title: Stop Skying It
description: Place an empty box or headcover just in front of the ball at tee height; swing without hitting it to shallow your angle of attack and stop skying drives.

title: Trail Arm Pitching Drill
description: Practise pitching using only your trail arm to develop a controlled body pivot and prevent flippy wrists; encourages proper release.

title: Hold the follow through
description: Hit 5 shots with your choice of iron and hold the follow through. If you’re chunking or topping shots, this will force you to be on balance and swing through the ball. Hold the follow through for 5 seconds.

title: One‑Handed Chipping Drill (Voice Caddie)
description: Chip balls using only your lead hand to firm up your wrist and encourage a shoulder‑driven motion for crisp contact.

title: Keep It in the Fairway Game
description: Set boundaries on the range to simulate a fairway and aim to hit all your drives within those lines; track your fairways‑hit percentage.

title: Hip Bump Transition Drill
description: Setup: Place a small ball (tennis ball or similar) between your knees/inner thighs, holding it with gentle pressure. Take your normal stance with a mid-iron. Execution: Make swings focusing on the transition from backswing to downswing. At the top, initiate the downswing by 'bumping' your lead hip toward the target—this lateral shift should happen BEFORE you start rotating. The ball between your legs helps you feel connected and prevents your legs from getting too active too early. Key sequence: Complete backswing → slight lateral hip bump toward target → then rotate hips open. The bump is only 1-2 inches—it's subtle. If the ball falls out, you're sliding too much. Hit 15-20 balls focusing on the hip bump initiating the downswing.

title: One-Handed Putting Feel
description: Setup: Stand over a long lag putt (30+ feet). Remove your lead hand from the putter and hold it with only your dominant/trail hand. Execution: Before putting with both hands, make 2-3 practice strokes with just your dominant hand, feeling how much 'swing' you'd need to roll a ball to the hole. Imagine you're rolling a ball underhand toward the target—how hard would you toss it? This engages your natural athletic instincts rather than mechanical thoughts. Once you've calibrated the feel, grip the putter normally and replicate that same energy. Key insight: Your dominant hand controls speed in putting—let it 'feel' the distance naturally. Use before every lag putt during your round.

title: 21 Putting Game
description: Place three balls at three, six and nine feet; make the 3‑footer for 1 point, the 6‑footer for 2 points and the 9‑footer for 3 points. First to 21 points wins.

title: Fat Drill — Lead-Side Pressure Shift
description: Setup: Place a folded towel or headcover on the ground about 2 inches BEHIND your ball. Use a 7-iron. Ball position should be center or slightly forward of center. Execution: The goal is to hit the ball WITHOUT hitting the towel. To do this, you MUST shift your pressure (weight) to your lead foot BEFORE starting the downswing. Feel like 70% of your pressure moves to your lead side at the start of the downswing, while your head stays back. This forward shift moves your low point ahead of the ball. Key checkpoints: (1) At the top, feel pressure shift toward lead heel, (2) Hands lead the clubhead through impact, (3) Divot should start AFTER the ball position, not before. Practice 20 swings in slow motion first, then gradually add speed. Goal: Make 10 consecutive swings without touching the towel while taking a small divot in front of the ball.

title: Left Shoulder to Chin Feel (Nelly Korda)
description: Deal with overswinging? Think about starting your downswing when your left shoulder touches your chin. Nelly Korda tip

title: Bunker Rectangle Drill
description: Setup: In a greenside bunker, draw a rectangle in the sand about 4 inches wide and 8 inches long. The front line represents where your club should ENTER the sand (about 2 inches behind the ball). The back line is where it should EXIT. Execution: Practice swings WITHOUT a ball first, focusing on entering at the front line and exiting at the back line—taking a consistent rectangle of sand each time. The club should splash through this entire rectangle. Once consistent, add a ball positioned in the middle of the rectangle. Key technique: Open clubface, aim left, swing along your body line (not at target), and accelerate through the sand. The ball rides out on the cushion of sand. Hit 15-20 shots focusing on consistent entry/exit points.

title: Swing Under the Alignment Stick Drill
description: Put an alignment stick into the ground or using a range bucket (see video) to force yourself to swing with a shallower angle of attack and an inside to out path. This helps to promote a draw with your driver and irons and avoid slicing.

title: Divot Pattern Awareness
description: After hitting irons, observe your divot direction and depth. Adjust your swing path and angle of attack to produce straight, shallow divots that point toward the target.

title: Follow Through Drill #1
description: Setup: Take your normal stance with a mid-iron. Execution: Make full swings and hold your finish for 3 full seconds. At the finish, check these positions: (1) WEIGHT: 90%+ on your lead foot—you should be able to lift your trail foot off the ground. (2) BELT BUCKLE: Facing the target or slightly left of it. (3) CLUB POSITION: Wrapped around your body with the shaft touching your lead shoulder/neck area. (4) BALANCE: Completely still and stable, not falling backward or forward. (5) TRAIL FOOT: Up on the toe with only the tip touching the ground. If you can't hold this position, something in your swing is off (usually deceleration or poor weight transfer). Practice: Hit 20 balls, holding each finish for a 3-count. This builds commitment through the ball and proper release.

title: Halfway Back Drill #1
description: Setup: Take your address position with a mid-iron. Have a friend watch or set up a camera behind you (down the target line). Execution: Make slow backswings and STOP when your lead arm (left arm for righties) is parallel to the ground. At this halfway-back position, check that: (1) The club shaft points parallel to your target line (not left or right of it).
